speakeroldname: Hon. E. N. RHODES (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I could answer that question with greater accuracy, Mr. Speaker, if I knew when the interim supply bill, which is now in the Senate, will be passed. I would anticipate, however, that it will pass the Senate on Tuesday night, and we might have royal assent Wednesday so that the money would be available to pay the salaries in question.

speechtext: The house, in committee of ways and means, resumed from Wednesday, May 3, consideration of the resolution of the Minister of Finance to amend the Income War Tax Act, Mr. MacDonald (Cape Breton South) in the chair.

Paragraph 3 of this resolution reads:	'
That the exemption for a dependent child or grandchild be $400.
This makes no reference to age. Has the age limit been changed at all?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There has been no change with regard to the age.

I believe the age limit is twenty-one years. Under pre-j

sent conditions I know many people who have educated their sons and daughters, but those children are unalble to find work to-day, and though they are over the age of twenty-one years they are still at home with their parents. It costs just as much to feed and clothe a boy or girl of twenty-two, twenty-three or twenty-four as it does a child of eighteen or nineteen, and under present conditions, when these young people cannot find anything to do and their parents are compelled to support them, it seems rather unfair that they do not get any exemption in regard to income tax.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think it must be borne in mind that we have gone a considerable distance as it is. In the earlier stages the exemption applied only to those under the age of sixteen. It was then changed to eighteen and subsequently, whether wisely or not, to the full age of twenty-one. I can understand and sympathize with the cases to which my hon. friend has referred, but I think it must be borne in mind that we must legislate in matters of this kind for at least approximately normal conditions, and we should not put into a statute of this kind methods which are designed to meet a peculiar and abnormal and, we hope, transient situation.

The Minister says that we should legislate for normal conditions, but it is obvious that the government is now resorting to certain taxes to meet conditions that are not normal. There are people in this country with children over the age of twenty-one, who very often find these younger members of the family coming back home when they cannot find work, with the result that the parents have to look after them. In many cases young people are charged with the responsibility of taking care of relatives such as aunts, grandmothers and others. Surely we are facing abnormal conditions to-day, and in taxing incomes the minister should bear this fact in mind, all the more when we see that in the province of Ontario and in other parts of Canada as well the taxpayers have to pay income tax not only to the dominion but to the provincial authorities as well. I think the minister should give this matter a little more consideration and recognize that we are faced with abnormal conditions at the present time.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The exemption in respect
to children is based on the presumption that they are dependent, and I think it can be said with equal force that a child over

Income War Tax Act
twenty-one years of age is presumably not dependent. Even if a law could be devised which would permit of exemptions in the case of those over twenty-one years of age, it would be opening the door to very wide abuses with respect to many children over the age of twenty-one who might be alleged to be dependent but who in fact were not so. I think we have gone as far as we ought to go in limiting the age to twenty-one.

Under section 4 it is
provided that the exemption for a dependent parent, grandparent, brother or sister shall be the actual amount expended by the taxpayer up to a maximum exemption of S400 for each such dependent person. I would point out to the minister that a man might have a son of twenty-five or thirty who because of physical incapacity might be absolutely dependent upon him. Why not make some provision with regard to such people?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
There is a distinction
between parents or grandparents and children who are dependent because of physical disability, but a vigorous boy or girl of twenty-one is not to be considered in the same category. The presumption is that a child over twenty-one years of age is not dependent on the parents for sustenance.

I notice that it is
covered elsewhere.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am informed that if the child is physically or mentally incapacitated the exemption holds.

Will the minister explain
for the benefit of the committee and of the people of this country the principle on which this schedule has been worked out. Would it be correct to say that it is on the principle that the rate of taxation should increase with the increase in the income itself?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The schedule as set out
has been evolved as the result of experience not only in its application but in its effect upon those who pay. It is not worked out on the principle of a percentage increase on income but on the basis of the dollars paid by the individual or the corporation as the case may be. We cannot overlook the relative rates of income tax in Canada compared with the relative rates in the republic to the south of us, and in that connection I would point out that up to a substantial proportion in the various grades in the schedule it will be found that the total income tax payable under these rates is higher than that which obtains at the moment in the United States.

In the first few items
in the schedule the rate increases apparently one per cent with each increase of one thousand dollars of income, but by the time you reach the last items in the schedule the increase of one per cent in the rate occurs with each increase of fifty thousand dollars in income. I think the principle contained in the first part of the schedule might have been continued right through, that is to say, increasing the rate one per cent on each increase of one thousand dollars in income as in the first part of the schedule. That would be much fairer to the people generally. I do not see why a lower rate of increase in the tax is carried out ia the schedules affecting the higher income. I suggest that the minister should not follow the example of the United States; we ought to draw up a complete income tax schedule to suit our own Canadian needs, and it would be better to impose a higher tax on incomes in excess of one hundred thousand, dollars. If this were done we could do away with a good many taxes that are so oppressive at the present time, such as the sales tax discussed the other day. The tax now before us is the best place to make increases. The principle contained in the act which the Prime Minister introduced two or three years ago but later withdrew, of increasing the rate of tax one per cent with each one thousand dollars increase of income, would be the ideal method, continuing that until it reached ninety-nine per cent on the ninety-ninth thousand dollars of income. Let us adopt that as an emergency measure to meet some of the deficits of the country. If we are to increase taxation that is the form it should take.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
If my hon. friend were to apply in stages the percentage increase in income tax as he suggests, he would find that even if there were those larger incomes, they would in effect be practically wiped out. I think it is very unjust to take the case of a man with a small income and state that his tax will be increased by perhaps three hundred per cent because of the provisions of this bill. A man with an income of $2,500 would have paid $2 tax under the old schedule; under the new, he will pay $15. There is an increase of 750 per cent which may sound alarming when considered in terms of percentages, but in fact his tax has been increased by only $13. Looking at it from that angle, which, is a practical angle, this proposal does not seem unreasonable. If we t taxed all incomes of $100,000 and over even
Income War Tax Act

to the extent of confiscation, the result to the treasury would be practically negligible because such incomes are a very rare thing in these days.

I did not want to suggest that there should be confiscation of anybody's income. The tax which I suggest would leave these very wealthy men with an income of at least 850,000. I am suggesting this only as an emergency measure. I think this would be a better means of obtaining revenue than by the taxing of buns, which we discussed the other day. I do not think the minister has given any justification for leaving the tax on the higher incomes as it was. He states that it is similar to the tax in the United States but I do not think we should go to that country for guidance in connection with our income tax.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
May I say to my hon. friend that I did not attribute to him the argument in favour of confiscation. I, was using that merely as an illustration from my own point of view. I was referring to the yield which might be expected from such a tax.
I agree with my hon. friend's suggestion that we should not be dependent upon any country for the principle which shall govern us in our own legislation. However, it must be borne in mind that this country is in close contact with the United States. Money is such a sensitive and rapidly movable commodity that if we attempted to tax incomes out of line with the taxation in the United States, we would very soon find that our capital was migrating across the line. We have to legislate with that difficulty in mind.

There is another suggestion I would like to make to the minister. I think he should endeavour ,to arrange a conference with the representatives of all the provinces to discuss this matter of income tax. Some of the provinces impose an income tax while a great many municipalities do likewise and it may happen that citizens may be required to pay three different taxes. If there is no consultation between these different taxing bodies, incomes may be taxed to the point of confiscation. I do not want to see that happen. I should like to obtain the minister's interest in this matter of a conference.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I may inform my hon,
friend and the committee that this subject was raised at the last provincial conference. As a result of the discussion a committee was appointed composed of the higher officials of the different provinces and the dominion, i
fMr. Rhodes.]
They are now at work upon this subject and I hope that as a result of their labours some understanding will be arrived at. In any event, we will have their report within the next two or three months.

Replying to a question
asked by the hon. member for Maeleod (Mr. Coote), the Minister of Finance stated that incomes of $100,000 and upwards were very scarce. I obtained some figures six months ago which gave the number of such incomes as 132, showing an increase from 75 in four years, 1928-1032.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My bon. friend must bear
in mind that those figures are for incomes of 1931. I can assure him that the incomes for 1932 were very much less and I think I am safe in saying that for 1933 they will be still further decreased. I had that fact in mind when I made my statement to the horn, member for Maeleod. The figures disclose that the total number of incomes, not of $100,000 and upwards but of $50,000 and upwards were 614. This was the number returned in 1932 as being applicable to incomes of 1931. I venture to say that this figure will be very substantially reduced for the year 1933.
Has the minister the total number of incomes of $100,000 and upwards?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am advised by the commissioner of income tax that the policy has been not to give out these figures. The reason is this: these incomes are very Tare and to give out the figures would be indicative of the incomes of individuals.

For the last ten or twelve years we have been able to obtain these figures, and I was able to obtain them as late as six months ago. Even if the figures showed that only one individual had an income of this size, I think the people would have a right to know. By what reasoning does the minister suggest that it is not in the public interest to give out this information.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
For obvious reasons the
practice has been not to make public the incomes of individuals. I think that is a sound position to take. When the attempt was made to find out bow many incomes there were of $100,000 and upwards, the question first was: How many in Canada? Then, how many in a province? Then, if in a province, in what city? It reached the point where you might just as well ask for the man's name. Naturally the department has resisted efforts of that kind and I think quite properly so.

Income War Tax Act

But if the question is
confined to the number within Canada and does not embrace a small area, it seems that the government is simply holding back information for which hon. members have a right to ask. I cannot appreciate the wisdom of the course 'taken by the government, nor can I see why the minister objects to giving, not names-I am not asking for names-but the number of people in Canada with certain incomes.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
There is no objection to
giving that information, and if the hon. gentleman would call at the income tax office, I am sure he would be given it freely.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
It is all
printed.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Yes, my hon. friend can
get the information. I am sorry my officials do not have it here, or I should give it now.

I just want to take this opportunity of stating that this type of statistics is available and I have no doubt it can be secured. But I wish to go further and register my protest against secrecy in connection with income tax returns. There should be the same freedom of information in Canada as there is in other countries, particularly in that to the south of us. After all, the minister must remember that in conditions such as these through which we are passing, more and more thought is being given to the causes that bring about such an unequal distribution of national income. A growing sense is invading every mind that interests itself in the subject, that this inequality of income is not necessarily the result of superiority on the part of the individual, but is due to advantages he is able to acquire by the possession of special privileges from governments, provincial and federal, and for other reasons including rather shady trickery in connection with commercial corporation life. The sooner this and other governments realize that they stand themselves as part of the destructive forces of modem society and modem parliamentary practice by hiding the facts that should be disclosed and not uncovering conditions that should be definitely stricken out of the society of our country, the better. As long as governments take the position of sheltering those people who without question are securing more of the national income than that to which they are entitled, just so long do governments place themselves in the position of being defenders of an unequal and unjust social order.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I can only say that, so far as I can ascertain, the result of experience has been that governments in all countries have found it to be in the public interest not to disclose the affairs of private individuals. An attempt to do so was made in one country and publicity was resorted to, but as a result of the unfortunate repercussions which arose from that policy, they reversed themselves and reverted to the policy which had obtained previously and which has obtained since in all countries.
What really were the unfortunate repercussions?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not know it is incumbent upon me to give that. All I can say is that in the judgment of that country it felt the experience had been unfortunate. I am not in a position to give my hon. friend the mental processes by means of which the government of that country arrived at that decision.
That is strange. The minister gives the experience of the United States-'I think that is the country to which he refers-as the reason we should not do this in Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I did not, not even by inference.

Then I fail to follow the reasoning processes of the minister. I cannot see any meaning in the statement unless it is intended to be imferentially that. But leaving aside the United States or whatever other country was referred to, I would like the minister to give on his own behalf the real reasons the public should not be given this information. I think we are entitled to have the reasons. The minister simply says that the experience has been unfortunate in some other country, but he will not say why, and he gives no reason why the experience should be unfortunate or undesirable in this country. We expect him to give some particular reasons that such a course is undesirable, but the minister so far has not done so.
I take it that there is a growing conviction that the wealth of Canada is not properly distributed, and that owing to purely conventional or artificial arrangements in society, some Canadian citizens are able to enjoy very large fortunes while others are on the bread line. We have our tariffs, our special privileges of all kinds and financial manipulation which is permitted, if not in some cases almost encouraged by the government. Through all these means certain people are enabled to make large sums of money. On the other
Income War Tax Act

hand, some of those same people who have
made the money are drawing, through their ownership of bonds, enormous revenues directly from the public. Within the last day or two we have been discussing a tax on sugar and other necessities of life and this house has been asked to impose upon the common people of the country who are struggling to keep their heads above water a still greater burden in order to contribute indirectly or directly to those people who have more than they should have. That is the way in which a large number of people are beginning to think of things. It seems as if the government is undoubtedly contributing very largely to the popular unrest and to the destruction of our so-called democratic institutions when the wealthy are permitted to continue as they are doing and are shielded by the government in their actions. The minister has yet to give any reason for publicity of this kind not being given. This whole question arose because we simply wanted to get some information for statistical purposes. We cannot get it even when the information makes no disclosure of the names of individuals. Personally I join with some other members in asking for more than that.

The minister has just stated that the reason the increased percentage on the ratings by this year's amendments is higher on the lower incomes than on the larger is that it is feared that capital may leave the country.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No.

That is what I gathered from the remarks of the minister. The 500 per cent increase on the lower incomes plus the reduction in exemption, the reduction as regards single persons being $200 and as regards married persons being $400, makes a heavier burden on the small taxpayer. The same percentage of increase has not been carried into the higher incomes. I have frequently heard the statement made that the reason the higher incomes are not taxed according to the same percentage is that capital will leave the country. That attitude is unfair. If that is the case, what is the excuse other than what the minister has said, namely, the necessity of revenue, for taxing the lower incomes so heavily? I believe in the income tax; I do not for a moment desire to say that incomes should not be taxed. This form of tax is the fairest we have imposed upon us. May I say that I am not very much concerned about it; I do not pay very much, but at the same time I cannot see any 
reason for the inequality. I do not blame the present minister for making that statement; it has been made before in the house. It seems to me that if we are going to have an income tax it should be applied on a fair percentage basis from the lower to the highest incomes quite irrespective of any effect that it may have in diverting capital from the country. I think that bugaboo is raised too often. There should be a fair percentage of the incomes taken all along the line, not a five hundred per cent increase just in one case, as the minister mentioned, and particularly at a time when the Minister of Finance in order to raise revenue has to resort as he has done in this budget to increased taxation that falls upon those least able to bear it. If an individual has a large income I think his income should be taxed according to the same rate as the man with a lower income, and I rise to protest that that is not being done at the present time. Certainly it is not being done now because the minister himself has informed us that there has been a five hundred per cent increase in the income tax in one grade, but he says that only means raising the tax from two to fifteen dollars, and that therefore, after all, it is not so great. Nevertheless it is a five hundred per cent increase, and it is just as difficult for the individual to provide that additional taxation as it is for the man with $40,000 or $50,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
May I say to my hon.
friend from West Edmonton that he entirely misapprehended my reference to the United States.

I did not
refer to the United States.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I only referred to the United States in answer to a question raised by my hon. friend from Macleod who urged that we might have still higher income taxes.
I was not referring to the individual tax paid in a given schedule. I might point out to my hon. friend from West Edmonton how impossible it would be to apply a fixed percentage. The case I cited was of an increase of five hundred per cent. What would he do in the case of a man who is already taxed fifty-six per cent of his income? How could he increase that man's tax by five hundred per cent?
There would be very few of them.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I do not think we have
any, but I am dealing with the schedule.

Income War Tax Act
If you cannot make an increase in his case, why increase the tax on the lower income? Just reverse the argument.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am dealing first with the hon. gentleman's own argument. He says that we have increased the tax five hundred per cent in one of the schedules, and asks why we should not increase it five hundred per cent in the case of the higher income. How are you going to make an increase of five hundred per cent in the case of the man who already pays fifty-six per cent of his income? That simply shows that you cannot deal in percentages in a matter of this kind. That is why I said to my hon. friend from Macleod that the gradations were not based on percentages but upon the amount of money which the individual could afford to pay to the treasury.
Coming to the question of lowering the exemptions, my hon. friend thought that bore more heavily on the man with a lower income. Strange as it may appear, the exact opposite is the faot. It bears far more heavily upon the higher incomes than upon the lower because the higher incomes are affected through all the various stages, and in the final analysis the man who pays higher income tax has his income tax increased by a very large sum because of the lowering of the exemptions of income tax.

I did not
follow the argument of my hon. friend in one or two matters. He suggested as one reason why secrecy should be maintained in connection with income tax information that the practice in that regard in the United States or some other country had been found distasteful and unsuitable. My reading in connection with the matter has not been possibly as extensive as I should have liked, but from what information I have been able to gather the real reaction in the United States was a sense of injustice on the part of the general public and a sense of deep inconvenience on the part of those who had the high incomes which were disclosed. In other words, it made those with the higher incomes feel a little ashamed of their position, and very properly so. My personal view is that in an orderly society any man who possesses an income out of all relation to that of the masses of bis fellowmen ought to have a sense of shame and disgust. He ought to recognize that it is not his wealth. Goods of that kind should never be regarded as his. It is the surplus wealth produced by those who may have been in his employment or in the industries from which he draws his profits.
So far as I am concerned the argument of the minister with regard to the flight of capital, if there was an increase in the income tax, is not tenable. We have not had that experience in Canada where income tax is imposed by some of the provinces and not by others. If the minister's argument were sound, why did not capital flee from the income taxing province to the province where incomes are not subject to taxation? There are other illustrations that might be given.
I have no hesitation in saying to the minister and the government that I think it is the duty of the government under present economic conditions in Canada, where we have such a terrible problem of increasing unemployment to meet, to confiscate all incomes over $50,000. Any man or any family that cannot live a luxurious life at present price levels on $50,000 does not deserve to possess more than that. It is plenty for any family. It is an ample allowance, and as it was made through the community effort of the entire state and never through the individual's own efforts-that is the most ridiculous argument anyone could put up, for no man could earn that amount alone; it depends entirely on the community-I would strongly recommend an income tax that would go to the point of confiscating all incomes over $50,000 as long as an emergency of this kind lasts.

Mr. Chairman, I am opposed to these new taxes, especially as they affect the workmen, the farmers who are forced to sell their products at ridiculous prices, and the unemployed whom the government should relieve. I am quite aware that the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes) requires revenues to balance the budget; however, in order to succeed he should call upon companies or people who are in receipt of an income to supply the necessary funds and not upon citizens who possess nothing.
A number of suggestions made by members in the opposition are worthy of consideration and, if they were given a trial it would help the hon. Minister of Finance to raise the necessary funds for the administration of this country. In a speech which I delivered in the house on April 14, 1932, with reference to the ten per cent cut in salaries of civil servants, and which was to effect a saving of $8,000,000 to the government-such were the contentions-I stated at page 2022 of Hansard:
If the government actually requires these $8;000,000 to balance its budget, why call upon the small wage earners instead of requesting those who are making large profits and are in
Income War Tax Act

a better position to put up the money, for a year only? Why not increase the tax on profit from 7 per cent to 50 per cent, after deducting what the act allows for living and overhead expenses. I am quite sure that millionaires and high financiers, who boast of being so patriotic when they force small wage earners to pay, would be willing to help the government to balance its budget, since it would only be a matter of one year.
The present budget contains new taxes which are not popular and levied in numerous instances on citizens vVho should be exempt of such imposts. The tax of 2 cents per pound on sugar will raise a revenue of $20,000,000. The hon. Minister of Finance replying on May 2, 1933, to a question of a member on this side of the house, page 4513 of Hansard, stated:
My hon. friend wants to know what these imposts will yield. Our estimate is that altogether they will yield $57,000,000 but that figure will be subject to change, because there have been some variations.
Mr. McIntosh: That includes $20,000,000 from sugar ?
Mr. Rhodes: I have given the figure that was in our minds at the time the budget was brought down. I shall now direct my remarks to the tax on sugar. I know it is not popular; no tax is popular.
Further he repeats:
The sugar tax will not be popular; I realize that.
It certainly will not be popular during an election. At page 4516 of Hansard, on the same date, the hon. minister replied to another member:
My hon. friend has suggested that the tax should be reduced. If we reduce this tax we must make up an additional sum by some other form of taxation.
The hon. member for North Waterloo (Mr. Euler), at page 4517 of Hansard, May 2, 1933, stated:
Now I come to the question of sugar. I think by this time the minister is convinced that this is not a popular tax; it strikes at everyone in the country.
And the hon. Minister of Finance replied ;o him by the following question:
Mr. Rhodes: Can my hon. friend name a popular tax?
At page 4527, the hon. Minister of Finance, in reply to the hon. member for North Bruce (Mr. Malcolm), added:
Mr. Rhodes: Well, who pays the tariff? The people in this country pay. Hon. gentlemen discuss that phase of the question as if they were going to relieve the people of the country of the burden of taxation.
Mr. Malcolm: The tariff is paid by those who are able to pay.

The hon. minister made the following statement at page 4558 of Hansard :
Mr. Rhodes: However, if the committee would give unanimous consent I am content that the list should be printed in Hansard. Perhaps this would be a good time to do so, because Wednesday is a short day, and we would not be unduly encumbering the record.

The hon. member for Charlevoix-Saguenay has just returned to the chamber and I am reminded of a question he asked and which I inadvertently failed to answer. I know his absence was necessary because he happens to be the chief whip of the opposition. The budget further imposes other taxes which are too numerous to enumerate. As one may judge by the above quoted list, the hon. Minister of Finance has thought proper, this year, to tax certain staple commodities among the primary necessities of life and to increase the sales tax by 6 per cent on other articles. However, there was already last year a tax on many articles the list of which is too lengthy to enumerate here.
After having closely examined the budget,
I find that a large number of my constituents whom I have the honour to represent in the house, will have to face further taxation; they cannot afford it as the wages of the working class, throughout the country, have been cut 50 per cent and work has decreased 75 per cent since the government has assumed power. As to the farming classes they can neither afford this new taxation since they are selling their products at ridiculous prices.
Judging from a number of years' experience in business, I can realize that the hon. Minister of Finance requires revenues, however,

I want to put in a word,
not for the large income but for the large families. I have seen the tax changed two or three times and I come from a district where incomes are not large but families are. In the province of Quebec, and I am glad to know that in other parts of Canada as well, Canadians have the habit of raising large families, and I think the exemption with regard to children should be graded; the same rate should not be paid by the man and woman with one or two children as by parents who have families of ten, twelve, fourteen or fifteen. The greatest asset of the oountry is the home, and the greatest asset in the home is the child. We should encourage large families. I do not think I can give a better answer than that. Turning to other countries, we find that in Great Britain the exemption to the married person is only $750, and so far as children are concerned, the first child has an exemption of $250 while for every other child it is only $200. So that, bearing in mind these various considerations, I think that on the whole it may be said that we have reached a fair figure. Certainly, under existing conditions, $400 is reasonable.

The minister has introduced

he said that these pensions under certain circumstances would be taxable. I am willing to admit that in that speech, acting for the government, he went too far. On May 3, the hon. member for North Waterloo (Mr. Euler) brought to the attention of the minister inequalities which, in his opinion, existed in paragraphs 5 and 7 of the Income War Tax Act amendment resolution. I would like to know whether the minister has given any further consideration to the representations of my hon. friend. I want to submit to the minister, in supporting the complaint of my hon. friend, that a 12J per cent corporation tax cannot be any more just than can an even rate of income tax and that the only way whereby I believe he can correct the inequality pointed out by the hon. member for North Waterloo would be to have some graduation in the corporation tax of 12J per cent. The minister realizes, as do all other hon. gentlemen, that small family limited companies are not in the generally accepted sense of the term corporations at all. The convenience of operating one's business under a limited credit charter is very great. It allows in case of death the willing of the interest a man may have in his business to his heirs without the official winding up of the business. As a result through a great many years the practice has grown up in this country of forming limited companies of small private businesses. Under our legislation these small limited companies are treated as corporations, and there is no difference in the rate of taxation on these small companies and on a large corporation whose stock is broadly held.
The hon. member for North Waterloo has pointed out that Should any one operate a private business where the total earnings were $5,000, he would pay $126, but the same business in the form of a limited company would pay $713. A private business earning $10,000 would pay $546, but if operated as a corporation or limited company would pay $1,667. It makes no difference whether salary is credited or not. I am taking the case where a man takes the profits out of his own business. I think the minister realizes that considerable inequality does exist in that regard, and I suggest to him that the only way I can see of correcting it is to modify the corporation tax by having the corporation tax graduated, as is the income tax, with a maximum of whatever the minister decides, whether it be 12-J or 10 per cent. The fact that a straight 12J per cent is taken from the corporation first, and then the owner has to pay income tax on the dividend, means that if you operate as a limited company you are 53719-2934
paying three times as much taxation as if you operate as a private business. I would ask the minister if he has considered any possible amendment.

Yes, a reasonable salary,
say of $3,000. So that even in the case cited by my hon. friend from North Waterloo and referred to by my hon. friend from North Bruce, you have the comparison of the company paying $357.50 as against the individual paying $120. But I might point out to my hon. friend that there are other incidental things to be borne in mind. If it is an incorporated company there must be some advantage in being incorporated.
Convenience largely.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It might be convenience,
but it must also be borne in mind that in the case of an incorporated company the individual owning it derives all the privileges which go with incorporation. In other words, if the venture should prove unfortunate the total assets which would be available to the creditors would be the amount of capital in the business, whereas if the individual conducted that business he would be liable for all the assets he had. So whether it is done for convenience or for other purposes, all of which might be equally lawful and worthy, the fact remains that it is to the advantage of the individual to be incorporated rather than to conduct his business as an individual. Otherwise, he would not be incorporated. That being so, the difference is not so great as to cause any undue worry.

The minister knows better than I do that the withdrawal of the private family corporation privilege is what has caused this inequality to exist, as was pointed out by the hon. member for North Waterloo. In spite of what has been said with regard to the advantages of a limited company in freeing a man from the danger of having to hypothecate other personal securities in time of financial stress, I do submit that the general idea of taxation seems to be to get after corporations. Provincial taxes on corporations are mounting, and I am afraid that the result will be that a great many charters will be given up. Many small businesses which have been operating as limited companies will find it impossible so to operate, and the taxation derived from companies will be lost to the provinces as well as to the dominion. For that reason I would submit to the minister, without wanting to hold up his resolution at .all, that I believe the subject is worthy of considerable study. I believe the inequality could be corrected by making some graduated scale that would put taxation charges on small corporations back to where they were under the family corporation privilege.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I shall be very glad to
give consideration to the matter, and if any remedy can be found without doing injustice to corporations as a whole I shall be very happy.

May I, Mr. Chairman, revert to the question under discussion a few minutes ago? First I would like to indicate my unqualified approval of the suggestion of the minister to remove the income tax exemption from pensions. This does not affect the small pensions and small salaries, the men we are endeavouring to protect. It will only apply where the total income comes within the range of income tax. But it brings us to the proposal which the minister put forward that was afterwards withdrawn, and I must confess that with somewhat mixed feelings I watched both the introduction and the withdrawal of that proposal. Taking it on the whole I was glad that the proposal to suspend the payment of all pensions to civil servants in receipt of the full salary of their position was withdrawn; yet at the same time I recognize, as so many have recognized, that there are and have been many apparent injustices and anomalies throughout the service that not only should be corrected if possible but that unquestionably cause a great deal of heartburning and disturbance amongst the public and amongst the returned men themselves. I refer to cases of men in receipt of substantial salaries and performing responsible work and being at the same time in receipt of substantial pensions. I am not going to mention any names, but those of us whose work has brought us into contact with pension matters have seen a great many cases that I think are obviously unjust. As the hon. member for Antigonish-Guysborough said, where you find a man in receipt of a one hundred per cent disability pension, or indeed any substantial rate running from seventy-five per cent up, who at the same time is in a position the duties of which are responsible and onerous and drawing full salary, I think it is obvious to anyone that either the man is not entitled to that high disability pension or he is not qualified to perform the onerous duties of a high salaried position. I think there is no question that these cases scattered through the service bring to the mind of many people the inevitable contrast, which the minister recognizes, between the position of these men find that of other men whose services were just as great, whose disability is just as great, although it was impossible to prove its attri-butability; and who have neither pension nor

Income War Tax Act
employment. That tremendous and striking contrast has undoubtedly caused a great deal of disturbance and trouble.
On the whole I am glad that the minister withdrew the proposal, not because of the effect on these men with good incomes, but because of the effect on large numbers of men in the lower grades of service, who are just able to make it go with their small pension and small salary. It has been said, and quite truly, that the pension is supposed to make up the difference between a man's present earning capacity and that which he would have enjoyed had he not gone overseas; to make him stand on a par with other men. It was said by some that any man who is earning the full salary attached to some of these positions must have his earning capacity unimpaired. That is not the case with all men receiving disability pension, there are many men in the position they are in on account of their disability, who but for that disability would have been qualified to occupy a much more difficult position and earn a much higher salary, but who because of their disability are able to- perform only light duties, so they are low in the salary scale. They would have Suffered, particularly as many of them were using that small pension to pay for the soldiers' insurance, the only way they could provide for the future of their families. The withdrawal of that pension would have necessitated the dropping of the soldiers' insurance.
But when the minister says that the matter is not finally settled I am with him. I agree that the sendee itself-I am not speaking now of the whole pension scheme-the service itself should be examined, and each of those cases of men in receipt of a pension and a salary should be dealt with individually, should be examined into and the anomaly removed if possible. I think no one will accuse me of being unsympathetic towards the returned men, I think my record in the house will establish that. I have sometimes been accused of being over thoughtful of their interests. But I am satisfied from what knowledge and experience I have, and assuming that the cases with which I am familiar give a fair cross section of the whole, that if the pension payments all through were to be dealt with with absolute justice there would be a very considerable saving; probably four or five million dollars could be cut off from our pension payments. But I am of the opinion that that four or five million dollars would not be saved to the country, but would be paid to those who are not at the present time receiving what they
should receive if absolute justice could be done.
Our difficulty has been this, the minister referred to it and I agree with him, that although our purpose was right and we have done our best, parliament has been meticulously careful to withdraw pension matters from any connection with politics, and I think parliament has succeeded. I think no government and as far as I know no member of parliament haS been guilty of mixing politics and pension matters. I have been on the committee every year there has been one and I certainly would not have known at any time to what party any member belonged from his efforts in the committee. But one thing that has been overlooked, and overlooked perhaps to a greater degree by the returned men and their friends than any others, is that just to the degree that you eliminate politics in pension matters, to that degree you nullify any influence that any private member or the government itself may have over pension administration. To the extent that you eliminate politics you take away from parliament and from the government the influence which sometimes should be exerted over pension administration, and it is left wholly to the officials themselves, to their sense of justice, to see that pensions are properly administered. I sometimes wonder if we have not gone almost too far in our desire to eliminate political consideration wholly from pension matters. However I do not want to go into that question now, I simply want to indicate my complete approval of the minister's suggestion to apply the income tax to all pensions where the total income comes within the range of income taxation. Also I wish to indicate my agreement with him that this question of pensions to civil servants in receipt of salary, also settled for the moment, is not settled finally, but that the anomalies I have mentioned will be removed in the only way possible if justice is to be done, that is by going through the whole service with a fine toothed comb and dealing with each case on its merits. You cannot go right through with one great sweep without perhaps doing more harm than good. When that time comes I am certain that every member in the house interested in the welfare of the returned men will interest himself in seeing that those who should have pensions get them but those who should not should have them taken away.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I would like to say a
word arising out of what has just been so
Income War Tax Act

well said by my hon. friend from Red Deer.
I think we all recognize that no one in the house is more entitled, from his experience and his service, to speak for the returned men than is my hon. friend. And few if any are better qualified than he to do so. I concur almost in toto with everything my hon. Mend has said.
The reason I rose, Mr. Chairman, was to say that with respect to the proposals originally brought down in the budget we were met with the objection on the part of those who spoke for the different organizations that it was a violation of contract, and that was a difficult argument to meet. But here is where I met my first disappointment, and I should not be surprised if my hon. friend and myself are on common ground in that respect: I asked them if it would not be fair to agree that this should have application only to those in receipt of a salary in excess of 12,000, $2,500 or some similar sum. They still interposed the objection that it would be a violation of contract. Then I came back with this: I said very good, we will observe the sanctity of contract even though to do so will cause an injustice to individual returned soldiors who to-day have neither pension nor salary. Why not from now on, with regard to those who come into the service hereafter, make it applicable only when it goes beyond the sum of $2,500 per year, or $2,000 or whatever sum might be agreed upon. To that proposal they also objected, and if I may say so without reflecting upon them in any way, in my opinion they exercised bad judgment.
I think it would have been a case of justice to the returned soldiers who, because of the application of that principle, might hereafter have an opportunity for employment in public service which otherwise would be denied them. For that reason I am doubly glad to hear the remarks of my hon. friend from Red Deer, and I hope that when another year rolls -round we may be able to apply that principle, which I think would be fair to all concerned.

That objection was
brought to me, and I could not but agree that it was a powerful objection. There was a contract; we did agree in every phase of our pension legislation that the pension should not be taken into consideration in this way. But this also is an underlying principle of the pension legislation-and I made the suggestion-that the pension is paid because of disability. That is, a man with a disability which detracts from his earning power by 20 per cent, 30 per cent, 80 per cent or 100 per cent is paid a pension to bring him up to par, to make up for that deficiency. It is

obvious that if a man suffers from a disability which impairs his earning powers to the extent of 80 per cent or 60 per cent, he cannot earn a full time salary at a full time job. If the pension is held sacred we might say to him. "If you are only 50 per cent capable you will only receive a 50 per cent salary, so you may take either the full salary and a smaller pension or the full pension and a smaller salary." Then we would be doing the fair thing and no contract would be broken.

I agree very largely with what the Minister of Finance said, and I think the hon. member for Red Deer predicated his remarks on a wrong assumption. Rightly or wrongly the parliaments of the past decided that pension would be paid according to a man's ability, to earn a living in the labour market, that is, with pick and shovel. It is quite obvious that a man may not be able to earn much of a living with pick and shovel though he might be 100 per cent efficient in many other lines of business. I think we must bear that in mind.
I do agree that an injustice is being done the country when we have a public servant as instanced by the hon. member for An-tigonidh-Guysborough, drawing a salary of $10,000 a year and a pension of $2,500. I do not think this country is under any obligation in a case of that kind. I am at a loss, however, to understand how that could happen. My recollection is that the maximum pension in the case of a private soldier was fixed at $60 per month, plus so much for his wife and so much for each child. I was wondering if the proposals of the minister could not be applied to officers, because I do not think many of the private soldiers will come under this taxation scheme in any case. A man with a total disability only receives $720 a year, so he would not come within the application of the income tax in any way, even with a liberal allowance for his wife and children. I do believe, however, that the returned men feel very strongly in the case of men drawing large salaries and large pensions. I do not think the elevator operators, for instance, should be taxed at all; I do not see how they could be taxed because I do not think their total income would be sufficient to bring them under the schedules, but I do think something should be done to protect the treasury if cases exist such as that mentioned by the hon. member for Antigonish-Guys-borough. In my opinion we do not owe any man, no matter what his services may have been, a return of $12,000 or $13,000 a year.

Income War Tax Act
May I say, Mr. Chairman, that for many of us it was a privilege to go overseas. It was an experience upon which we can look back and which we will never forget; we would not have missed it for anything. Personally I look upon that experience with a great deal of pride; I would rather have missed almost any other period of my life than the service I saw in the trenches. I think every returned man should be sufficiently interested in his country to share the burden that is being carried to-day by every man, woman and child in Canada, and I should like to see the minister do something with regard to these people who are receiving both high salaries and high pensions. I do not think that is just or equitable. As I said before, I do not see how the private soldier is going to be affected by this legislation; I do not think his pension and salary together would bring him under the schedules, but if his combined income is sufficient he should pay his tax.
With regard to the first proposal I have just this to say: I never saw how it could be defended, and I do not see that yet. A man went to the front and lost an arm, a leg or an eye, and the country said, "We will give you so much money to compensate you for your loss." Then we say to him, "If you enter government service and do the work that is done by another man, you must work for less money." That is penalizing him because he was injured in the war, always provided that he can do the work as efficiently as the other man. I do not believe that proposal could be defended. I do say to the minister, however, that he must do something with regard to these men drawing large pensions and large salaries. I think it is his duty to do so, and personally I will be quite willing to defend that policy at any time, because I think it is right.
It is our job to find some way of putting that suggestion into effect.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Amendment agreed to.

Before this resolution
carries, Mr. Chairman, I should like to ask the minister a question with regard to paragraph 11, which reads:
11. That a tax of 5 per centum shall be imposed at the source on all dividends or interest paid or credited by Canadian debtors to non-residents of Canada.
I understood there were some amendments to that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Perhaps my hon. friend has reference to the statement I made in the house on March 31.
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The provisions contained in that statement are carried out to-day, but it is done administratively. No amendment to the resolution is required to effect that purpose.

What method is the
minister taking to carry out the promise made on March 31?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Will my hon. friend put his question in another form.
Do sections 11 and 12 cover the new interpretation of the tax on dividends of non-residents?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Dividends are still taxable when paid to non-residents,-
All dividends?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: -and interest only to the extent that it is paid in Canadian funds. There will be one or two minor amendments but they will be presented when the bill is in committee; it will not be necessary to amend the resolution. I am advised by the law officers that there is no necessity to amend the resolution itself in order to carry out fully the provisions as outlined in the statement I made on March 31. There will be some minor changes which it is thought wise to have made in committee of the whole on the bill.
Will the minister indicate those minor changes?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Perhaps I might table a summary of the proposals as applicable to this tax, which I think will answer succinctly every question which is likely to be submitted by my hon. friend from North Bruce or anyone else. I have copies in both English and French and I will table a few now, and more will be available as hon. gentlemen desire.

The minister will remember that when the hon. member for Shel-burne-Yarmouth was speaking after the introduction of the budget he said he did not know very well how to criticize these provisions in the budget inasmuch as he had no idea what they would be when the budget was finally revised and amended. It was pretty common gossip on the street that on March 31 telegrams had reached the minister that the London stock exchange had deleted all Canadian securities from the official list and pro-
Income War Tax Act

hibited further dealings, with the result that on getting this word from London the minister took fright and set about making amendments. I am told that the idea of the minister at the present time is to exempt from payment of this tax and interest all Dominion government bonds held by non-residents, but that other bonds, provincial or corporate, will still have the tax applied. I understand also, if I am correctly informed, that all bonds payable in the currency of any other country are to be exempt. It seems to me that the exemptions are so extensive that the amount of tax that will be collected will not be considerable enough to justify the complications that will arise in the minister's endeavour to collect them.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Let me say this, particularly with reference to that part of my hon. friend's remarks touching what was said by the financial critic of the opposition, the hon. member for S'helbume-Yarmouth. It must be borne in mind that in this tax we are breaking new ground so far as Canada is concerned, and it is quite obvious that in doing so we shall encounter difficulties here and there. Therefore I make no apologies whatever for any changes which may have been found necessary from the original proposals-none whatever. It is certainly nothing new in this country to have changes made in the budget, because we have not had a budget in years that has not been changed materially. Instance after instance could be cited, in the case of governments which were supported by my hon. friends opposite, and I am not the least bit worried about criticism of that sort. The man who does not make mistakes never does anything, and a government that would be so timid that it could not proceed for fear it might have to retrace its steps would not be worthy of the name. So far as I am concerned therefore I have not the slightest feeling of diffidence in making changes if they are for -the better. I may say to my hon. friend that the consideration we had in mind was this. Britain for years has imposed taxes of this kind-
Certainly.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
-but they are in the
happy position of being a rich creditor country.
Quite so.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The United States also for some years has imposed similar forms of taxation, and it too is a powerful creditor country. Now, we in humble little Canada attempt to impose the same sort of taxation and of

course we must dodge the big stick. Why? Because we are a debtor country, and a small country. It is true we had to relinquish some of this tax, largely by reason of the circumstances I have outlined and partly because it was pointed out to us that we had to honour contract obligations; and I regret that my hon. friend could even be able to refer to the incident with respect to the London stock exchange, because their attitude was not in keeping with that solid, sterling character which we have always associated with Britain, especially touching matters of finance. But they went off at halfcock-
They certainly did.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
-whereas our friends in
the United States who were subject to the same tax kept their heads, and were calm and cool about it, prepared to wait until they found out what the full incidence of the taxation meant. Our friends in London, however, became so hysterical that they went completely up in the air. They suspended operations. They did not wipe Canadian transactions off the boards but they suspended operations, "don't you know," until they could find out what the various proposals meant, in the meantime, no doubt, fully expecting that they would frighten the poor colonial.
Which they did.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Which they were able to
do in part. If my hon. friend derives any comfort from that admission, very well; I make it freely.
I am sorry.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am happy to say that
we have held a substantial portion of the tax and it will yield a substantial sum to the treasury.

You should have held
it all.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
In its essence, it is a fair
tax as it enables us to pay into the treasury of Canada money which hitherto has gone into the treasuries of other countries. If a resident of Great Britain or the United States pays this tax he will receive full allowance for hds payment.
That is when he pays the British tax?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
When he pays his tax in
Great Britain. I must say that the attitude taken by the London stock exchange seemed to be singularly unfair especially when it is borne in mind that we are asking only for a humble five per cent while the mother coun-

Income War Tax Act
try asks for just exactly one quarter or twenty-five per cent under similar conditions. However, these are the facts and the circumstances and I recite them without any limitation or evasion whatsoever.

I think the candor of
the minister is to be commended. My criticism of the action taken by the minister is that there was a want of courage. He should not have been frightened by a gun at half cock. As he points out, there was no justification for this action by a country which itself taxes non-residents twenty-five per cent. It is a fair tax. The investor in a foreign country must realize that there are two entirely separate fields in which a government may operate. Because a government sells securities does not mean that it is going to give up control of taxation. The minister was perfectly justified in proposing this tax but I do not think he was justified in receding from the original position which he took.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: In part.

Yes, in part. I think
the tax was fair and I think it was needed for revenue. I join with the minister in saying that the action taken by the London stock exchange to delete Canadian securities from the list in order to frighten the Canadian government was unfair. If I had been in the minister's place I would have gone through with the taxation as originally proposed.

In connection with the collection of the tax upon bearer bonds, would the minister advise the committee what position an individual would be in who had not sufficient total income to necessitate the paying of the tax or who had already declared the income received from bearer bonds? Would the tax be deducted by the bank and then application made for refund?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: A man who cashes a coupon in Canada of a bearer bond payable in Canada will be called upon to attach a certificate of ownership. No money will be deducted at the moment of payment but the certificate of ownership will be attached to the coupons and will subsequently come to the income tax office. If the individual does not come within the range of those who pay income tax, no tax will be collected, but, on the other hand, if he does come within the range, a tax will be collected. The advantage of the system is that it will prevent evasions which have hitherto taken place in the case of those who have not declared their whole income from bearer bonds.

In order to get at the
interest rates paid on bonds there must either be reflotation or taxation. The minister's first attempt at taxation is very fair and modest and should not be complained of by anyone. There is no doubt that there is a great difference in value in the interest received to-day and that received in 1928 when the bonds were sold and there is a necessity for increased taxation upon the interest paid or a lowering of the rate of interest. As far as I am concerned, I would be entirely in favour of having the original proposals in the budget remain in force.

Has the minister ever
thought of having a more simple income tax form? I think most hon. members have received complaints about the forms from farmers and others, who have had to fill them out.

Have the farmers any
bonds?

Not so many bonds but
still many of them are compelled to fill out the forms. My suggestion would be that a form of questionnaire be sent to the farmers. This could be filled out and returned to the income tax office and if the individual was liable for tax, the income tax form could be filled out at a later date.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I can quite understand the attitude of mind of an individual who is confronted for the first time with an income tax form. I do not know whether my hon. friend has ever seen the form of ballot used in some of the states of the United States, but I shall never forget the first time I saw one of these. It was just about the fiercest document I have ever seen, filled with all sorts of diagrams and hieroglyphics and whatnots. Apparently those who had become familiar with its use were not awed by its presence. I think the same thing is true to a large extent of our income tax form. While they present complexities and difficulties to one who sees them for the first time, be gradually becomes familiar with their use. I do not think it is the form that bothers us so much as the figure which appears at the lower right hand comer. The income tax officials who have been able to profit by the experience they have gained in years gone by tell me that they feel that the form is as simple as it could be having regard to the safeguards which must be utilized in the collection of a tax of this character. I can say to my hon. friend and to all other hon. members of the committee that if they have
Income War Tax Act

any suggestions of a workable character to offer in the way of simplification of the form, I am sure the commissioner of income tax will be ready to consider their adoption if they are at all workable.
Mr. M-UNN: Referring to the bearer bond coupons, I am one of those who believe this, if carefully handled, will return to the coffers of the dominion and provincial governments a great deal of money. My opinion is that in handling the tax this year, the government should go back and see why the man was not able to pay t'he same tax last year. I hope the minister will have his officials instructed to have this made retroactive, because I really think a great deal of money has been lost to the dominion treasury through people who are dishonest in making up their returns.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It was part of the object I had in mind when these proposals were brought down that not only should we collect from the individual this year, but we should find out what he was doing with his income in previous years. The law is ample to enable us to do that. It may transpire that Mr. A, in making out his income tax return this year, discloses that he has certain bearer bond coupons on which he has not made returns previously, and as a result his income bears a different proportion from the one hitherto disclosed. The question will then be put to him: When did you purchase those bonds? There will be no difficulty in finding out when the purchase was made, and if it is disclosed that he purchased those two, three, four or five years before, he will be called upon to recoup the treasury to the extent he has defrauded it in times past.

I wonder whether the minister would clarify paragraph 16. I have been reading it over and I cannot make out the real sense of it, particularly where it reads:
Provided that in no case shall such interest or taxes be apportioned against the taxpayer's income from his chief occupation or business.
Just what does that mean?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Perhaps I could answer my hon. friend's question, at least in part, by referring to a provision in the bill itself which will be based upon this resolution:
Section 6 of the said act is amended by adding thereto the following paragraph:
(h) Carrying charges of property the income from which is exempt, except to the extent that such carrying charges exceed the exempt income.

The explanation on the corresponding page of the bill is as follows:
This section provides that the carrying charges of productive property producing
income-
That would be property real or personal; it might be bonds or it might be something else. -which is exempted from taxation, such as tax-free bond interest or dividends received by one company from another shall be applied first against such exempt income. Any excess of such carrying charges may be applied against income other than the income from the taxpayer's chief position, occupation, trade, business or calling.
I do not know that I can make the matter any clearer than that.

I wish to draw the minister's attention to paragraph 12. The purpose of that is that if a man cashes a dividend cheque in the United States at a premium, he shall have to pay 5 per cent, not on the premium, but on the whole dividend. That may be all right, but it will be noticed that in the income tax return in the form that you have to make out, there is an item inserted in which you have to show any income you have received from premiums obtained in that way, so that you will have to pay not only twice, but three times. Supposing the premium on a specific cheque of $100 is 10 per cent. You do not pay 5 per cent on the $10; you pay 5 per cent on the whole dividend. Then when you come to make out your income tax return, you again have to pay whatever your income tax rate is upon the amount you have received in that way. That is certainly paying it a second time. I do not know whether the minister understands me.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think I do.

Then there is the third effect. I submit it is not in accordance with the usual custom to charge for that at all. Should it not be called principal increment? For instance, if a man bought something in the United States, as he often does in the course of a year, he has to pay a premium on the money and he does not receive any allowance for that in his income tax return, so he pockets the loss. In the one case it should be called capital increment, the same as in the other it would be called capital loss.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
To answer my hon. friend's last question first, our principle of taxation in Canada has been only to tax income. We have never taxed increment. I think the experience of the past two, three or four

Protective Service Salaries
years has abundantly proven that in that respect we have adopted the right principle, because to-day, despite the condition of the world and conditions in Canada, we are in receipt from our income tax of a total yield which is comparable with the tax which has been received in other years, whereas to take the example in the neighbouring country to the south where losses are to be taken into consideration in making up income tax returns, the result has been that the yield of their income tax has shrivelled to only a fraction of the normal amount. The result is shown in the enormous deficit which they had there last year.
The government does not tax increment? .

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No.
But this is increment.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
We do not take into
account the increment at all; they do.
I claim that this is increment.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Well, coming to the first question, when the man pays his 5 per cent tax, the amount that he pays, although paid upon the total, is less than the premium he receives.
It might not be.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Then the tax' will not be applicable; that is the answer. When in making up his income tax returns he comes to show the amount of premium he has received, that premium as shown would be less the 5 per cent which he has already paid.
But not less the other sums he may have paid as premiums if he had bought stuff in the United States during the year.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We could not cover a case of that kind.
Does the minister not consider the premiums as increment?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I would not think so. If anyone were to consider as increment the amount of purchases he has made, our income tax returns would disappear very rapidly.
I am referring to that specific case only; when you tax the increment, you ought to allow for the decrement, it seems to me.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Apart altogther from the question whether the tax is applicable to increment as such, tihere is the question whether it would be wise policy for us so to regulate our income tax as to make it to the advantage of the individual to purchase in a foreign country to the exclusion of his own. That question would also arise and it has no reference to tariff or protection or anything else. The fact of the matter is that that is what we would be doing.
