Mr. G. G. COOTE (Macleod) moved the second reading of Bill No. 81, to amend the Interest Act.
He said: Mr. Speaker, under section 91 of the British North America Act interest is one of the matters placed under the control of the Dominion parliament, and the present Interest Act is chapter 102 of the revised statutes of Canada, 1927. The bill I am introducing proposes to repeal section 2 of that act, which reads:
Except as otherwise provided by this or by any other act of the parliament of Canada, any person may stipulate for, allow and exact, on any contract or agreement whatsoever, any rate of interest or discount which is agreed upon.
Because of the very difficult economic conditions existing in Canada many persons are being compelled to pay very high rates of interest, and this bill asks that a maximum rate of five per cent be established in the Interest Act. Perhaps I -might read the bill to make this clear. The preamble states:
Whereas excessive rates of interest are being charged on loans on mortgage, agreements and contracts; and whereas it is advisable under present conditions to fix a maximum rate of interest in Canada, applicable to loans, contracts -and agreements of every kind: Therefore His Majesty, by and with the advice and consent of the Senate and House of Commons of Canada, enacts as follows:-
Then the bill proceeds:
1. Section two of the Interest Act, chapter one hundred and two of the revised statutes of Canada, 1927, is repealed, and the following is substituted therefor:-

Interest Act-Mr. Coote
"2. (1) Notwithstanding anything to the contrary in this or any other act of the parliament of Canada, the rate of interest shall not exceed five per centum per annum, and no person, corporation or company shall stipulate for, allow, exact, reserve or collect a rate of interest or discount greater than five per centum per annum, and in no case shall a higher rate of interest be recoverable.
(2) Every person, corporation or company who or which, directly or indirectly, takes, accepts and receives a higher rate of interest than is authorized by this section shall incur a penalty equal to twice the value of the moneys, wares, merchandise or other commodities lent or bargained for. Such penalty may be sued for and recovered in any court of competent purisdiction by any party injuriously affected, on proof of such excessive interest."
This principle of a maximum rate of interest is not entirely new in Canada; it was in force in the four provinces which originally came into confederation, and I think it remained on the statute books until 1890, when all the acts were repealed by a bill introduced by Sir John Thompson. Under the old act in Ontario and Quebec the maximum rate of interest was fixed at 6 per cent, except for insurance companies and religious, charitable and educational corporations, which might exact a rate not exceeding 8 per cent. Included in that section was a penalty for violation of the act amounting to treble the value of the goods or loan. In Nova Scotia the maximum rate was established at seven per cent, except with regard to loans on personal property or on personal responsibility, when rates up to ten per cent were allowed. In New Brunswick the maximum rate was six per cent, and the penalty imposed for violation was the value of the principal sum or the goods covered by the loan.
The bill I am introducing does not attempt to deal with the rate of interest on existing obligations. That question was raised in a motion introduced by the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Speakman), and his resolution was referred to the banking and commerce committee for consideration. Apparently there is not very much chance of any action by the committee on that resolution during this session of parliament, but by this act it is hoped to fix a maximum rate of 5 per cent on obligations entered into in the future. According to a definition which I found in the dictionary to-day interest means money paid for the use of money loaned, or money paid for the forbearance of debt, and I am afraid that at present most of the interest that is being paid is for the forbearance of debt rather than for the use of money loaned. In many cases the money loaned has largely disappeared.
Interest is sometimes referred to as the wages of money. Money is a sterile thing; it does not increase of itself. I am not going to enter into a discussion at this time as to whether or not interest is something that can be paid; I know some economists and financial writers differ on that point. I would simply say that if interest is actually paid it must be paid out of production. This was so well stated by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens) in this house last year that I am going to quote his words, which will be found at page 1911 of Hansard for 1932:
-let us get this as clearly as possible- interest is not something that is made by money but something that must be taken out of the productivity of the country and paid upon the money that is lent.
In other words, Mr. Speaker, interest is paid out of production; that production is sold for money and the money thus obtained is turned over to pay the interest. The rate of interest which industry can pay depends upon the price of the product. Because of the fall in price levels during the past three years the payment of interest in some cases has taken two or three times as much of the product of industry as it did three or four years ago. This increase in the general burden of debt can be well illustrated by the fall in the index prices of commodities in Canada. I find that in the wholesale commodity index price level there has been a drop from 100 in 1926 to 63.6 in February of this year, a fall of 36 per cent. In the case of the general range of farm products I find a drop from 100 in 1926 to 43 in February of this year, or 57 per cent. In the case of field products there is a drop from 100 to 36, or 64 per cent. In the case of animal products the drop has been from 100 to 54, or 46 per cent, while in retail prices and cost of services, according to the government's index figures, the drop has been from 100 to 79, or 21 per cent.
In the light of the index figures I have quoted let us look for a moment at farm mortgages. If a farmer paid the interest on his mortgage in field products, in 1926 the interest on $2,000 at 6 per cent would be $160, or 160 bushels of grain, whereas in 1932 the interest would be still $160, but it would require 440 bushels of grain. If the farmer paid in farm products generally it would take two and one-third times as much in 1933 as it did in 1926, and if he paid in animal products it would take practically twice as much. If it took ten steers to pay his interest in 1926 it would take twenty steers to pay
Interest Act-Mr. Coote

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
his interest in 1933. If it took one hundred pigs to pay his interest in 1926, it would require two hundred in February, 1933. This will give the house an idea of the increase in actual interest so far as it is measured in terms of production

and it is only with production that the farmers can pay. Precisely the same principle applies to industry generally. I want to quote again from the speech of the Minister of Trade and Commerce, because he put the matter briefly and clearly. At page 1911 of Hansard of 1932 the minister' is reported on this point as follows:
Precisely the same principle applies to an industry. Take one that has for its basic product copper, lead or zinc, operating in some manufacturing concern. Suppose they borrowed $50,060 three or four years ago. In the payment of interest on that money, where they formerly calculated an output of a given amount would serve to meet that payment, it would to-day take an output of two to three times as much to discharge the obligation.
Surely these illustrations prove that our industries cannot continue to pay rates of interest of six and ten per cent and sometimes as high as twelve per cent. I want to quote another passage from the same speech of the minister:
Let me turn to the third factor, that of interest. I say this advisedly; I say it after a good deal of study and thought, and I ask my hon. friends angularly opposite to accept it in regard to not only agriculturists but industrialists and merchants, because it is only by having some degree of sympathetic contact among the different branches of activity in this country that wo are going to make any progress. No agriculturist, no industrialist and no merchant can afford to pay ten per cent interest for the money he uses in liis business: it simply cannot be done; normal business will not permit of that rate of interest. Moreover, no bank can afford to take a loan at ten per cent, because it is too risky. When a loan justifies a rate of ten per cent, in my opinion it is too risky a loan for a bank to take at all and ought not to be accepted.
I heartily agree with that.
Whether or not that can be covered by arbitrary statutory legislation is another question. That can be discussed next year at the revision of the Bank Act. I am laying down what I consider to be sound business principles directly affecting our welfare, and the same principles are operating in every corner of the world ki-day affecting the business of the world and affecting us along with the other countries. But I lay down the principle that a rate of interest around eight or ten per cent makes successful operation of the ordinary business activities impossible and unprofitable.
I am of the same opinion; I believe that rates of eight and ten per cent make the successful operation of any industry impossible and unprofitable, and it is partly for that reason that I am bringing forward this bill

to-night. The fall in commodity prices has reduced the purchasing power of the people engaged in these industries and this in turn has created unemployment. Thousands of workers, factory employees, salaried and professional men have had their income cut to the point where the tax paying ability of the people has been reduced by half. This has made the burden of some municipal and provincial government debts almost intolerable. The ability of large numbers of people to pay the interest on their debts has disappeared, while in many other instances it has been greatly curtailed, and in no industry that I can think of can they afford to pay interest at a greater rate than five per cent per annum.
I would again direct the attention of the house to the question of farm mortgages. According to the recent census in Canada these mortgages amount to over 8700,000,000. At the end of 1931, in respect of all mortgages held by insurance companies in the dominion, there were, in arrears of interest for one year or more, in Saskatchewan, forty-six per cent of the mortgages, in Manitoba forty-two per cent and in Alberta twenty-two per cent. It will be freely admitted I think that at the end of 1932 the percentage must have been much higher because of the low prices prevailing then. In many cases interest for three years compounded at eight or nine per cent is now arrears and the borrowers are asked to sign new mortgages in which these arrears have been added to the principal, so that the principal is being increased by from twenty-five to thirty per cent, and the people are being asked to renew these mortgages at rates of eight and even nine per cent.
There is a good reason for these large amounts of unpaid interest. Take the case of wheat producers. There are certain cash costs that must be incurred in the production of wheat and only after these are met can interest be paid. This applies to many other farm products. The selling price very often has not been sufficient to cover the cash cost, and if the interest has been paid the money has come from borrowings on insurance policies or from the sale of equipment or young live stock which should have remained on the farm. In other words, the farmer has been compelled to pay interest out of capital equipment which it has taken him years to accumulate. Very frequently the interest has not been paid because the farmer could not secure it. The fact is that the payment of interest at five per cent is for the most part a greater burden to-day than the payment

Interest Act-Mr. Coote
of interest at twenty-five or thirty per cent would have been three or four years ago.
I have in my hand an editorial from the High River Times, which I think brings this point out clearly. It tells of a farmer who has been unable to pay interest because of low prices. He bought a section of land in Alberta in 1917, paying for it at the rate of fifty dollars per acre. I quote:
However, in 1917, prices were good, and the price waB paid on the strength of the excellent crop prospects. Unfortunately in August of 1917 the crop was completely hailed, destroying the revenue for that year through no fault of the purchaser. The following year, when wheat was still good in price, the yield was poor Owing to drought. And so on, through the ups and downs of succeeding years. In the meantime, as an accommodation to the seller, the farmer got a loan from a loan company, to pay off the large part of the amount owing. He has been struggling to hold on to the land and meet the demands of the loan company. Interest charges and taxes amounted to approximately $1,400, and in recent years it has been impossible to meet this amount. Last year the company foreclosed on him.
In the years since the purchase, this farmer has paid out over $40,000 on the original price of $32,000 (a top price by the way). Yet despite the payment of this $40,000, which represents the effort of the best years of a. man's life, he has been foreclosed, and now stands well up in years, stripped of the reward of tifteen years of labour.
He has been industrious and capable, keeping his farm clean and productive. He will probably be replaced by a man much less capable and experienced. The district has lost an excellent farmer. Moreover the man has been financially ruined through the curse of interest. There are many who maintain that under the wheat prices of the last three years, a farmer cannot pay 8 per cent interest, and survive. It is a legalized hold-up, condoned by the government.
Back in the war years, when wheat threatened to soar to $3 the government had no hesitation in stepping in and preventing exploitation of the buyer by forming a wheat board and holding prices to a maximum of $2 a bushel. To-day, conditions are even more glaringly awry, but now it is interest which is soaring far above the ability of the primary producer and normal citizen to pay. Why is there any more difficulty in bringing interest charges under control?
Not only have the inexorable demands of money lenders (demands sanctioned by government) brought financial ruin to thousands of Canada's finest citizens, but worse still, these demands tacitly supported by the government have produced discouraged and embittered citizens who know that under all laws of justice, they have been deprived of the labours of a life time.
I regret to say that according to all accounts a great many farmers have found themselves in the position of the man referred to in this editorial, and it is time that parliament took such action as lies in its power to restrict the rate of interest charged. Farm mortgages are 53719-294
being renewed to-day at eight per cent, and I believe even at nine per cent. Many machine notes carry interest rates of from eight to twelve per cent; buyers of automobile trucks and so forth, purchased on time have to pay interest rates running as high as fifteen per cent. The rate of interest paid on savings accounts has been reduced, so why should not the rates charged by banks and others be reduced. Eight, nine and ten per cent is being charged for bank loans. I received a letter recently from a man in Hamilton complaining of the loan companies in Ontario asking for higher rates of interest on mortgages now maturing than the rates paid some years ago. One case has been brought to my attention where a mortgage made in 1927 at seven per cent with a proviso that six and a half per cent would be accepted if the payments of interest were tendered on the due dates. speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
There is one phase of this question which I am sure my hon. friend has overlooked, and it is one of numerous considerations which have a bearing upon the principle of the bill. My hon. friend has been an advocate of a central bank. One of the strongest arguments that can be adduced in favour of the establishment of a central bank is that it could control the flow of ci'edit. My hon. friend knows full well that there is just as much danger in a policy of too easy money as there is in a policy which makes for dear money. The banks in the United States saw the danger of that great inflation movement, the stock market boom of 1928 and the early part of 1929, and they tried to stop it, the bank rate being raised to as high as ten per cent, if not indeed higher. I think perhaps a major feature which the advocates of a central bank claim for it is that, through its control of open market operations on the one hand and of rediscount rates on the other, it can make for a reasonable equilibrium of the ebb and flow of credit, and for a fair interest rate. If my hon. friend should fix a maximum interest rate of five per cent he would take out of the hands of a central bank the greatest lever it would' have to prevent just such an inflationary movement as occurred in the New York stock market in 1928 and the early part of 1929. If there were no other objections to this bill, I think that of itself would be sufficient to condemn it in the eyes of this house.
I am satisfied that my hon. friend could do no greater injury to those whom I know
Interest Act-Mr. Rhodes

he earnestly desires to serve than to have his bill passed in the terms in which it is drafted, because the effect would be to deny credit altogether to those who should have it. If they could secure any capital at all they could do so only through what I might call underground or bootleg channels, and if they got it under those conditions they would rate far higher than the open market going rate. I have been listening to the apostles of free trade so long that I have become somewhat tired. They are free traders when they are on the hustings and protectionists when they are in power. I wonder why they cannot be consistent. They have maintained a higher tariff than hon. gentlemen on this side of the house ever did. I should like the hon. member for Lisgar to listen to the words of a gentleman who was one of his own allies when he sat in the far corner of the house. I was a member of the house in 1925 and 1926. I am going to read what this gentleman says in his book and it will bear me out so far as the Liberal party and their tariffs are concerned. The whole thing is a joke. The Liberals are no more free traders and they do not practise free trade more than we do on this side of the house. This gentleman says:
The Liberal party was first elected to power in 1873. The issue was lower tariff with a view to ultimate free trade; it held power for four years. No alteration in the tariff policy resulted. It was elected again in 1896. The issue was still lower tariff, with a view to free trade; it was in office for five years: result, tariff unaltered. It was in power again in 1900. The issue was once more tariff reduction with a view to free trade; it held power for four years,-result, tariff practically unchanged. Reelected in 1904, held office four years, the tariff still unchanged. Again in 1908 the Liberal party was returned to office on a policy of tariff reduction; it held power another three years without results as to low tariffs. In 1921, the Liberals once more cape to power; policy, a gradual downward revision of the tariff; it held power until 1925-the result was that the tariff stood as before.
What is the name of the book?

I was in the house in 1925 when I saw the parade in front of this building and I heard the statement made from this side of the house when you occupied these seats, as to what you were going to do, and when you got those men nicely home, what did you do? You know very well what you did. You took the duties off parts for the automobile manufacturer and you gave them more protection than before. One of the manufacturers told me so in Oshawa. Oh yes, we went out after it and we got it, and now we are struggling to save this old ship from swamping. I believe the hon. Minister of Finance is doing everything that is honest and faithful, and why do hon. gentlemen opposite hold up the house and keep us sitting here when we ought to be home? speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
There is only one other item on the tariff list, Mr. Chairman, and that is item 6S2a, to which I have an amendment to move.
Customs tariff-682a. Net floats of aluminum, glass or cork, for use only in deep-sea or lake fishing, not to include floats for sportmen's use: British preferential tariff, free; intermediate tariff, free; general tariff, free.
In the budget provisions we included among the free items, floats of glass or aluminum.
The amendment I have is to widen that to include canvas floats as well. My hon. friend from Comox-Alberni made a plea that we ought to include trawl kegs and sinkers. May I say with respect to trawl kegs that I find they are made almost entirely by the fishermen themselves. They are a home-made product, and to the extent that they are purchased it is of advantage to the fishermen that they should be purchased from themselves. With respect to sinkers, they are made of lead and they are a home-made product also. Certainly they are to a large extent in the east. At all events, I am advised that on balance there would be no advantage to the industry as a whole to amend the item to include sinkers, and for that reason I have thought it wise not to do so. I therefore move:
That tariff item 682a as amended by resolution No. 2 of March 21, 1933, be further amended by inserting therein after the word "glass" the word "canvas."

The desire to include sinkers arises from the fact that it militates against both fishermen and manufacturers in this way. I have not the tariff item before me, but when these sinkers are attached to nets brought in in one complete entity, so to speak, they come in free. But many sinkers are used on the same net later on in the ordinary course, as the sinkers often get lost, and if the minister does not put the word "sinkers" in here he is hurting the Canadian manufacturer, which is not supposed to be his object. It is an inducement to the fisherman to buy his net from the United States complete -with all the sinkers and lines and floats, because then they come in free. But a great many fishermen do not want to do that. They prefer to buy just their web and the lines and sinkers, and then put them together themselves. The people who are in the business of manufacturing these articles are handicapped because they have to pay a duty on sinkers coming in individually and which they sell retail, or wholesale and then retail and the extra cost is of course paid by the fishermen, whereas when the sinkers come in with the net they come in free. While it may be true that in the maritimes, and possibly to a limited extent in British Columbia, the sinkers are made out of lead by the fishermen themselves, there is a regular standard sinker manufactured for the purpose, of a certain shape and with a hole in it to run the line through, which is quite distinct from the home-made article which the fisherman cuts out of a piece of lead. I cannot
Customs Tariff Amendment

see that it would do any harm to the revenue by inserting the word "sinkers." I was given to understand that we had a fair prospect of getting this inserted, and I so advised the fishermen. I am sorry to find it is not going to be accepted now. I have a letter here from a manufacturer quoting a letter from the department as follows:
Concerning the leads referred to in paragraph three of your letter, When attached to nets et cetera, provision is made in the act for exemption from sales tax on goods enumerated in customs tariff item No. 682, when under a class or kind and for the purpose stated therein. The exemption applying equally to similar goods manufactured or produced in Canada.
That is dealing with the sales tax, but the same principle applies. Last year the minister was good enough to exempt the sinkers from sales tax and I thought the same argument would have applied in regard to duty. I remember a delegation waiting on him, and I formed the opinion that we might have got a favourable decision then if it had not been for his desire not to open the tariff act last .year. Is it not possible that the minister might leave this over for further consideration?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I assure my hon. friend I have given careful consideration to this matter. speakerposition: subtopic

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, did not the minister promise to allow a debate on the stabilization fund proposal after we passed this?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My hon. friend is quite right. The understanding was that by unanimous consent discussion would take place in committee prior to report. The understanding the other day when we were in committee will be found at page 4560 of Hansard:
After we have eoncluded our several items in committee, and just before reporting, I should be perfectly content if by unanimous consent there should be a discussion in committee of the stabilization fund.
That was the understanding arrived at then,
. as against consideration that we would discuss it on a motion to go into supply, which would confine hon. members to one speech,

I will not detain the committee long; at any rate I will not go as far afield as did the hon. member for Marquette. I just want to reiterate a plea for the inclusion in the stabilization items of pilchard meal and pilchard oil. I brought this up before in a general way, but I lacked full information, and the Prime Minister said the door was left open for further details. I just want to put a few additional facts on the record.
The request is that pilchard manufacturers of British Columbia, which is the only place in Canada where they manufacture pilchard oil and meal, should have their products included in the stabilization scheme. In speaking of it the other day I made a mistake about the valuation of the plants. Thinking of the buildings only I said they would probably be worth $5,000 to $8,000 apiece, but I am advised I was wrong in that regard; I had forgotten the expensive machinery and boats. I am told that the investment will run in each case from $50,000 to $400,000. There are twenty-seven plants, and if you multiply that number by $150,000 as a mean, it gives an investment of over $4,000,000. The industry employs some 2,000 men. I would like to state one or two facts to show the desperate condition this once prosperous industry is in. Four years ago there were twenty-four plants running; last year there were seven. Four years ago eighty-six seines were operating, that would employ at least 600 men; last year there were only twenty-two. Four years ago the selling price per gallon for the oil was thirty-seven cents; last year it was eleven cents, a fall of two-thirds. Wages of fishermen per ton four years ago were $4 ; 'ast year they were $1.60.
In addition to the troubles they had at that time the government made conditions a little more onerous by putting a sales tax on fuel oil, which while it may be of benefit to the coal mines or to the revenue is going to make it more expensive to operate these plants. Hitherto the great market for pilchard oil has been in the United States, where they have a tariff against it of five cents a gallon. When the price is thirty-seven cents that is one thing, but when the price is ten or eleven cents it is a much greater thing, it amounts to fifty per cent. They state that there is no expectation of any sale in the United States this year; the only inquiries for pilchard oil now in hand are from Great Britain. The British market is an enormous one if they can get into it. Japanese shipments of fish oil to Britain last year were 4,000,000 gallons. They state that under present conditions unless something is done the industry is practically wiped out. You can imagine that if it drops from twenty-four plants down to seven it is nearly wiped out. It is impossible to reduce further the charter rates for fishing vessels; they are already so low that they pay only operating expenses. The pay of. fishermen and plant workers is also so low that a further reduction would result in their going on relief. The operators suggest that the only possibility is the inclusion of these products in the stabilization fund, and they say the cost would not be excessive. On last year's products it would amount to someting like $16,500, and probably would be much less now owing to the increase in the value of the pound. They ask also that pilchard meal should be included as well. That is part of the business. The price dropped from $54 a ton four years ago to $20 a ton. The United Kingdom is a market for that also.
I might also suggest as an argument in favour of it that the usual expression used concerning these things is "fish and fish products," and I think that was at one time in the mind of the right hon. Prime Minister, because my recollection is that he used it. But it has not been so expressed; it is only "fresh and canned fish." It is a question of these people 'having to go entirely out of business, in which case 2,000 white people will be thrown out of work and an investment of $4,000,000 will be almost thrown into the discard. The possibility of selling in the United States is negligible because, as I was saying before the right hon. Prime Minister came in, the duty in that country now amounts to about fifty per cent of the value. Formerly it was very much lower, but it is
Stabilization Fund,

a fixed duty and now it amounts to practically fifty per cent of the value. There is an enormous market in Great Britain, and under present conditions the expense to the government would not be very heavy. It is indicated that S16,500 would at least keep these remaining plants operating for another year, and I earnestly hope the government will give this question its serious consideration.

The hon. member (Mr. Duff) speaks of including lumber, and as there are large lumber interests in my district I might

Stabilization Fund

be expected to endorse his remarks. I understand however, at least I heard the Prime Minister say some weeks ago, that it was not intended to apply the stabilization fund to lumber because he had in view other methods whereby he hoped to benefit the lumber industry. I take it I am at liberty to guess or to suggest that that means some negotiations with the United States, and that is where we in British Columbia want the market. The stabilization fund might help us to get into the British market, but that would be like trying to make water run uphill. Our natural market for the second and third grade of goods we want to sell is right at hand in the United States; we cut the product the way they want it and they are accustomed to our standards. Putting the duty back as it was last year in the United States would do us infinitely more good, so far as the lumber business in British Columbia is concerned, than including that product in the provisions of the stabilization fund. That at any rate is my individual opinion. What I do want is to have pilchard products included in the stabilization fund. That would do us as much good as applying the fund to salmon. I do not hesitate to say that the stabilization scheme will be of material advantage to the canned salmon industry of the country, and I ain glad to express my appreciation of it; but the including of pilchards would do us as much good. A couple of thousand men are engaged in the industry. I have hopes in this matter, because the Prime Minister, speaking on March 24, said that the door was not closed against other agricultural and fish products. I hope therefore that consideration will be given pilchards later on.
How will this stabilization fund be put into effect? It does not appear that the Minister of Finance intends to bring in an act to carry it out. The money comes out of the general relief vote and I presume that an order in council will be passed. If it is done in that way will the minister publish the order in council so that everyone will know what is included and what the conditions are?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is proposed to bring the stabilization fund into effect by order in council, and it is intended that the widest possible publicity shall be given as soon as it is announced.
Is there any limit to the fund in dollars, in amount?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No.

Is the door still open for
other items to be included?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am sure the Prime Minister will carry out his undertaking in that respect.

I desire to support the
plea made by the hon. member for Antigo-nish-Guystorough on behalf of the people in his section of the country in connection with fish products. As hon. members well know, the largest item of export from Prince Edward Island is potatoes, but because of the embargo against this commodity by the British government, very little benefit will be derived by the producers from the stabilization fund if it does come into effect as far as Prince Edward Island is concerned. Some little benefit may be derived by the producers of cheese and meat products, but that is all. Strong representations have been made to the minister, not only from Prince Edward Island but from other parts of the country, on behalf of the silver fox industry. If any industry lends itself to the application of this stabilization fund it is the silver fox industry. Many people think that as this industry has been in operation for a great number of years it does not need any assistance, but many of the large ranches are not making a profit to-day. They are carrying on in the hope that they may get a break in later years. Shippers of silver fox pelts ship direct to the British market and separate accounts are kept, so that any money which might accrue through this fund would go direct to the shipper and not be absorbed by other interests. If the pound keeps on improving it may be that the government will not have to pay out anything through the stabilization fund. I suppose everyone would welcome that happening.
They should make it retroactive.

There is another factor
to be considered in connection with this industry. It is quite possible that the operation of the stabilization fund will increase the price of meats. As everyone knows, carload after carload of meat products are sent down to the maritimes from the abattoirs in this part of the country. If the price of meat products is increased, there will be an increase in the cost of producing silver fox pelts. If this industry is not included in this fund, its operations would react against it. I hope the Minister of Finance will give this matter his special attention.

Any cost that might
arise from the payment by the government of the difference between the existing rate of

Stabilization Fund
exchange and $4.60 has now been transferred in large measure from the taxpayers of Canada to the ordinary buyer of the pound when sold on the market. It would almost appear as though the action of the American government in abandoning the redemption of her currency in gold is putting the relationship of the pound to the dollar back to the position occupied when both the pound and the dollar were on a gold basis. Nor personally do I imagine that when the market settles the relationship between the pound and the dollar will differ very greatly from the relationship that existed at the time both currencies were on a gold redemption basis. Inasmuch as the margin between the present rate of exchange and $4.60 mentioned by the government is so narrow, I submit that in order to benefit alike all products, the government might without very heavy expense to the treasury apply the stabilization to all products shipped to Great Britain.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat has touched upon one phase of this matter which was in my mind some weeks ago when I spoke in the house and indicated that the door was not absolutely closed. We had some reason to believe that there would be an increase in the value of the pound in terms of dollars. Perhaps that increase has come about more rapidly than was expected by most people, and speaking to-night I should not care to indicate that I was of the opinion that it is at all stabilized. I suppose I should not say more than that the figure at which sterling exchange is selling today is not in my judgment the true measure of what the ultimate value of the pound, as stabilized, will be. However, that is only an individual opinion and has no particular value beyond being my own view of the matter. The circumstances which have brought about the rise during the last few days are perhaps not unknown to hon. gentlemen. All I can say is that if one were certain and could predicate with some degree of authority a fixed value, I believe my colleagues would agree, as I agree, with what has been said by the hon. gentleman. It was for that reason that we did not desire to express with too much certainty a limitation upon the articles which might enjoy the benefit of this fund, and that thought is still in the mind of the government. In particular is that so of the commodities which cannot in any sense be affected at this moment, that is, commodities which will not be in condition for export until much later on in the year. I ask the committee to appreciate our position in the matter. We determined that this was the proper step to take at 53719-295J
this particular time and we did this for reasons which I think most hon. members who have followed the trend of economic conditions will agree were apparent to every observer. Having done so, we contented ourselves for the moment with stating the articles to which it would apply. Those articles have been referred to to-night.
There are such items as apples, which has been pressed so strongly, about which we might be compelled to arrive at another conclusion in the light of crop conditions which may prevail this fall. The same is true with respect to pears, plums, and other fresh fruits which have been finding a market under very considerable difficulties in Great Britain. Apparently the hon. member for Antigonish-Guysborough has misunderstood the effect of the preference upon apples. I think the hon. member for Hants-Kings could represent more authoritatively the views of the apple growers of Nova Scotia. I think this was indicated by his vote upon the United Kingdom agreement. The fact is that to-day apples enjoy a larger preference in the British market than they ever have before. At the moment that preference amounts to $1.25 per barrel as against apples coming from outside the empire. The strongest pressure was exercized by Australia and New Zealand with respect to apples and only last week I was told in Washington that the Argentine is capable of supplying apples which because of seasonal conditions would not conflict with those from Canada. I fancy the former Minister of Trade and Commerce is familiar with the details of the Argentine production of apples. I can only say this: I desire to make it quite clear that the movement in the value of the pound sterling has made the amount payable on the limited number of items mentioned rather small, and contemplating as we did an expenditure much larger than would be involved under existing rates, if there is a stabilized value approximating one around the figures that we have had during the last few days, I will say it might be possible to extend the list, and substantially too. The Minister of Finance and various other members of the government have received applications with respect to a very considerable number of products. I do not suppose it would greatly interest the committee but as a matter of curiosity, the committee might like to learn the views of various Canadians as to the items that might be placed upon that list. speechtext:

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I am sorry the hon.
member for Lisgar has lived so long on the prairies that he is not able to understand the fish argument made by the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth and the hon. member for Comox-Alberni. But the only point I desire to make is that the matter has been considered and the question of determining the extent to which the reaction might be injurious rather than helpful has not been determined. It has not been settled that some assistance along the line suggested may not be given to the industry.
The hon. member for Lisgar suggests an artificial stimulus to industry. I can safely say that the cattle growers on the prairies do not look upon the matter in that way; they, represented at least in the other house by one of the ranchers from Alberta, do not hold any such idea as that. At a meeting of the Western Cattle Growers' Association, they passed a resolution stating that the action taken at the time it was, meant the salvation of the cattle industry on the plains. But if, as the former Minister of Trade and Commerce says, ordinary conditions bring about a value of the pound of $4.60 or any value approximating that, we shall rejoice that the necessity for relying upon the fund will have passed and that the conditions of trade in the world, world price levels and commodity prices generally will have ensured a return to some measure of prosperity that will enable the businesses to which 1 have referred to carry on at a profit and not under conditions that now exist.
I should have said that in regard to the pilchard oil industry there are special difficulties of which the hon. member for Comox-Alberni is no doubt aware. The experimental stage has undoubtedly been passed in connection with the use of pilchard oil, but the competition is such as to make it extremely

Stabilization Fund
difficult to predict with any degree of certainty what conditions may be within the not distant future. I suppose the hon. gentleman knows to what I refer.
With respect to lumber, the imposition of a revenue tax upon lumber by the United States was, as will be recalled by the committee, for a limited time only, and, if my memory serves me arig-ht, it expires next year. It was not a tariff; it was included in the revenue bill, and I think it is only fair to say that with the entire disapproval of the administration it was written in for very special reasons through the efforts of those who live in states contiguous to British Columbia and who are also engaged in the lumber industry. Undoubtedly the embargo placed by Great Britain upon the importation of Russian lumber during the last few weeks has had some effect upon the lumber industry in the eastern part of Canada. The distances are so great that the same benefit has not aocrued with respect to British Columbia lumber, but some benefits have arisen by reason of that in regard to the finer qualities of fir and lumber that, as I understand the matter, are used for finishing purposes in Great Britain.
The list that was submitted to the house of course embraces a larger number than thirteen items because, for instance, meats include a large number of items, such as:
Bacon and hams, shoulders and sides.
Beef and veal, fresh, chilled or frozen.
Beef and. veal, pickled in barrels.

That would be the classification involved in the use of the word "meats" with respect to the fund. The item of eggs involves three classifications:
Eggs in shell.
Eggs, dried.
Eggs, frozen.
The item of milk products embraces several classifications. I am afraid I have been very discursive in what I have had to say to the committee, but I desired only to make it clear that in the light of improving conditions with respect to the medium of exchange between the two countries we may be able substantially to broaden the list without increasing the expenditure.

My observation directed to the Minister of Finance with respect to the narrowness of the spread between the
existing rate of exchange and $4.60 was not based particularly on the belief that it is a wise plan to bonus all commodities exported to Great Britain, but rather on the fact that the amount of money involved being very much less with the narrower spread on account of present exchange rates, as mentioned by the Prime Minister, made it possible to extend this list to include all commodities. It is, of course, natural for everyone to have a desire to sell his commodities, whether abroad or at home, in terms of dollars with which he is accustomed to deal, and it is indeed desirable that our exporters should know how many dollars they will receive for any given quantity of their exports. It is dangerous for anyone to make any prophecy on the fluctuations of the money market, but I do feel that the rate of exchange in Canada to-day, being practically the same as it was when both England and the United States were on the gold standard, only indicates that so long as they both stay off the gold standard, or if they both come back on, the parity of exchange will not fluctuate violently from the present level of $3.90 to $4. Inasmuch as the benefits of this stabilization fund expire in March, 1934, and as between now and then the Prime Minister will have attended the world economic conference in London, I hope for the sake of the trade of the world that before next March some definite relationship will have been established between the various currencies of the trading nations. I do not estimate that the spread between the current rate of the pound and $4.60 will be very much greater than twenty or thirty cents at any time. I doubt if it will be that. To-day there is only the matter of a very few cents difference.
I do submit again that the government would be well advised to adopt the principle of giving this assistance to all exports so that the exporters may realize from the stabilization fund on their commodities, whether they be lumber, fish or any other commodity, unless through some drastic drop in the value of the pound the assistance could no longer be continued. The government, of course, has the right under the legislation giving them power to deal with emergencies to withdraw this assistance if they are not able to continue it.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: In Canada it was usually at par before Great Britain went off the gold standard. I think my hon. friend is confusing the $3.90. Par was $4.86, and the value in the United States, whether it be by cable transfer or on demand or thirty days, was usually somewhere between $4.80 and $4.90, par then being $4.86, while to-day it is only slightly over $4.
It is not quite $4.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: It ran to $4 at the close for a little while. So there is a discount of 86 cents on the American side. Here in Canada we ran to-day up to $4.52 as a maximum, I think, reflecting to a very large extent the difference between Canada and New York with respect to currency generally. I just correct my hon. friend because I think his observations were directed to the time when Great Britain was off the gold standard and America was still on.
That is so.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: What he said was when both countries were on the gold standard. It was just that, that I desired to correct.

Ever since this
stabilization fund was announced by the Minister of Finance I have been in somewhat of a dilemma to know upon what basis these thirteen commodities have been selected. "When the matter was under discussion shortly after the announcement was made I endeavoured then to find out the basis and failed. I will be more particular now with regard to what I have in mind.
Why were animals, for instance, chosen as one of the commodities, when we all know that anything paid out of the stabilization fund will be less likely to get back to the producer in respect of this commodity than of almost any other commodity of the thirteen you could mention? I do not need to mention the reasons. I might indicate, however, that the packing industry is pretty much one entity in Canada, and you have not the ordinary competition that you would get if there were a number of independent packers, although 
there are a few, of course. This exchange stabilization will not therefore reflect itself back as freely on animals as it would on many other commodities I might mention.
Again, why is cheese put on this preferred list and not butter? An attempt was made to explain that, but I certainly could not understand it. Cheese has been included among milk products but not butter. If cheese is made from a different kind of milk or a different kind of cow than butter I did not know that before. Milk products, of course, include both these commodities, and yet one gets the preference and the other does not. One is taken and the other is left for no apparent reason.
Then why should honey and maple sugar products be given this preference when both these commodities have already been given a substantial hoist because of the duty on sugar? All these saccharine products are affected by the sugar duty, consequently the tiny bee and the maple tree are very much in on this deal. There is only $16,000 worth of honey exported and $180,000 worth of maple products. A number of articles are mentioned in the return which I got from my hon. friend the minister, particularly on representations from the west, but those people had no idea under the sun when they were asking for these things that the government (was going to make a selection of thirteen articles and never include one of the cereals on the selected list or butter or many other articles I could mention. I could not imagine any more teeny-weeny pinhead way of dealing with a big national question than that which the government has adopted, waiting and waiting, dilly-dallying and shilly-shallying until almost there was no occasion for the stabilization fund, and then at last under the reflected glory of the president of the United States the government emerges with some tiny degree of credit in the matter.
May I ask one or two other questions for information which will enable us to talk a little more intelligently and a little more comprehensively on Monday if this matter again comes up then? I wonder what was the lowest figure to which the pound dropped since September, 1931? Could the minister tell us?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I would not like to give
a figure offhand, but I could get it.

Customs Tariff Amendment

I would be interested in having that. Then another question; why should canned frujt and canned vegetables be given the benefit of this stabilization fund while the raw products are not? It is true that some of these raw products would be too perishable to export, but the fact remains that when they are manufactured they come on the preferred list. That requires some justification, I think. Then in estimating the losses we must consider not only the enormous losses that have been sustained on farm products, but also those on factory, forest and everything since September, 1931. Now when there is nothing mudh to be done the (government comes along courageously to do something already done by nature. Let nature take her course! The law of the survival of the fittest always works, but it is a ghastly and costly process, leaving wreckage in its trail all over the country. The same with the law of supply and demand; it is sure to work, but what [DOT]happens to our people in the meantime?
These are some of the cogitations I engage in on this quiet Friday night, I do not know if I can continue in the same vein on Monday. Ju-st now the government is pretty quiescent; it knows it is vulnerable to attack on front and rear and on both flanks. If any flank is more exposed than another it is the rear, I think. I am not saying this threateningly, but if my bon. friends knew the condition of the country, especially of agriculture, the despair and distress that exist while they are dilly-dallying with this thing, I do not believe they would be able to muster a smile at all. I find great difficulty in being able to smile about it myself. If you notice, Mr. Chairman, I have been keeping distressingly quiet. You know what is said about the weather when it is very quiet; it indicates a storm brewing. I do not think there is anything like that in my case, but I feel terribly serious to think the government has waited so long to throw us even a wee lifeline. I have heard some supporters of the government telling each other what a lucky fellow that man Bennett is-

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: They don't know!

Possibly. Here he
is holding on to his wheat with the backing of the Dominion government, while the rest of us. with no backing behind us, had to sell
ours during last December at five bushels for a dollar. He hung on to his, but at the expense of those who had to sell. The cheaper it was the more we had to sell to get a bit of money to pay our taxes. All those things are still fresh in our minds, and will keep until Monday as far as I am concerned. I think if the minister would give us that exchange information by months from the time the pound went off gold, and maybe a month before, it would be of interest.
As to the canned vegetables, some of these of course could not be exported in the raw state, but somehow the manufacturers get in on these things pretty frequently. Of course if they passed the stabilization fund proceeds back to the growers it would not be so bad, but how much would be passed back? A great many of these products are controlled under a complete merger. A merger is not always a bad thing, but if they want to use it for bad purposes they can do so.
Another thing; will the minister provide us with an estimate of the number of commodities that we export to Great Britain? Thirteen are mentioned; I wonder if there are a thousand altogether. If there are thirteen hundred then at the rate of thirteen a year it would take one hundred years to get around to them. I do not think there are thirteen hundred, but there may be half that number, in 'which case it would take fifty years to cover the lot at thirteen per year.
